question: What keeps a Qualcomm SoC out of its lowest state on mainline?
found: Any processor or bus vote left up: on a QCS8550 handheld, aosd, cxsd and ddr stayed at 0 until the USB controller's interconnect vote and the PCIe and LPASS (audio) votes were released, then it reached the floor at about 23 mA (2026-10). A DSP that never sleeps holds CX up; on surya the audio DSP has not slept once. FastRPC helpers attached across suspend crash the audio DSP: postmarketOS stops hexagonrpcd's helper before suspend on the Pixel 3a, as we saw on surya (24 of 24 attempts with rootpd attached). Wi-Fi (ath10k) floods the modem's IPC interrupt and blocks or breaks suspend on SDM845; surya is reported to wake at random while asleep, cause unknown.

question: How does a Qualcomm phone reach its lowest power state on mainline?
found: Through s2idle and CPU idle, not suspend to RAM: the firmware offers no PSCI system suspend, so with userspace frozen the CPUs enter their idle states, the last one down takes the cluster power domain to its deepest state (PSCI OS-initiated mode, hierarchical CPU idle), and as the cluster powers off the application processor's RPMh sleep votes are flushed to the always-on subsystem (rpmh-rsc attached to the cluster domain). The always-on subsystem then lowers CX and DDR when no processor votes for them: CX collapse (cxsd), then AOSS sleep (aosd), the floor. The SoC counts each in its own memory (rpmh-stats, read through qcom_stats), so reaching the floor is measured, not inferred. Without OS-initiated mode the cluster domain would stay always on and the votes would never flush; surya's firmware has it.

question: How does a Qualcomm phone on mainline wake for a call or a message?
found: The modem's messages (QMI over QRTR on glink) are handled even in s2idle (IRQF_NO_SUSPEND), but userspace is frozen, so nothing rings. The kernel cannot tell a call from a signal-strength update: there is one switch, the IPCRTR glink device's wakeup (/sys/bus/rpmsg/devices/4080000.remoteproc:glink-edge.IPCRTR.-1.-1/power/wakeup), which wakes for every modem message. postmarketOS (now Nura) pairs it on the OnePlus 6 with ModemManager's quick suspend/resume, which quiets the modem's notifications before suspend and resyncs after; that fixed calls signalled late or lost. It is still not dependable: on OnePlus 6/6T and the Pixel 3a waking for calls is reported not working (with the switch on the phone wakes at once; open since 2026-10), and with it on every modem event wakes the phone. surya's modem sits at the same address (remoteproc 4080000), so the same path applies; a SIM card is needed to prove it.

question: How else have phones got deep sleep that still rings?
found: Android's own kernel: Ubuntu Touch runs officially on surya through Halium with the vendor's 4.14 kernel and Android's opportunistic suspend (wakeup sources and autosleep, which mainline also has), claiming a day and more - deep sleep that works, at the price of the vendor's kernel and blobs and nothing upstream. A separate power-management core: Crust on the PinePhone sleeps the whole Allwinner SoC (about 80% less power) and the separate modem wakes it through its RI line; Qualcomm's always-on subsystem runs signed firmware, so nothing like Crust can be written for it, and its modem is inside the SoC. Push through sleep: only partly solved anywhere (PinePhone: WoWLAN pattern matching plus an RTC wake as a safety net). The postmarketOS SM7150 page lists suspend as working with no measurement behind it; we found no published standby current for mainline Qualcomm phones.

question: What already exists for measuring a phone's health on the phone, shipping it there, and letting agents work with it - in postmarketOS and in our own commons?
found: postmarketOS (docs.postmarketos.org/pmaports/main/ci/hardware-ci.html): tests ship as small shell files in postmarketos-test-* packages (suspend by an RTC wake alarm; bootrr, which checks per board, keyed by the device tree's compatible, that every expected driver probed) and run in the initramfs CI hook on their hardware CI (CI-tron gateway); surya has no bootrr board file yet. In the commons: the package conveyor (linux-package-distribution-oco/conveyor) already builds static aarch64-musl binaries with signed provenance and plans signed Alpine repositories for postmarketOS (cv-apk) and machines that receive updates, the phone next (cv-machines-refresh); agent access (creation-guidelines/agent-access-oco) plans every tool's structured door offered over MCP, in Rust with rmcp, naming devlab among the first (aa-two-doors). In lab-tools itself: devlab test ran surya's checks from the lab over SSH, health kept a baseline of what ever passed, watch ran health after each boot from the lab - nothing ran on the phone by itself, and the checks were one surya-specific file.

question: How do SM6150/SM7150 'bolero' boards and their siblings (SM7125 atoll, SM6115 bengal, QCS615 talos) record their microphones on mainline and open stacks, and what does the vendor's own model say?
found: Working on mainline, legacy q6afe firmware: SM7150 davinci (sm7150-mainline PR 60, open, -62 dBFS floor) and surya (pulpoff/linux-surya; and linux-phone-oco since 2026-11-17), both through analog mics on the WCD9375 -> TX SoundWire -> TX macro DEC (SWR_MIC) -> TX_CODEC_DMA_TX_3. The SM7150-specific trap: its TX SoundWire controller has one dout port, which shifts both the master port numbers (inputs from port 2) and the controller's DAIs (capture is DAI 1); SM7125, the template, has none, so its <&swr2 0> is right there. Nobody streams the VA port on SM6150/SM7150; both trees declare a VA link and leave out the DCODEC vote this ADSP refuses. The vendor (sm6150 bolero, qcom,va-without-decimation) uses the VA block only for MCLK, the fs counter and DMIC clocks, clocked from the TX macro's MCLK through bolero's mclk mux, and routes every TX and RX path to VA_MCLK; mainline gives the same through the VA macro's fsgen clock on the TX macro. No open implementation of va-without-decimation exists - only a board with real DMICs on this family would need it. SM6115/QRB4210 (Linaro RB2 v3) records DMICs through VA_CODEC_DMA_TX_0 with the DCODEC vote: not a template here. QCS615 upstream (2026-05) is AudioReach with an external DA7212, headset mic only. postmarketOS ships no microphone support for SM7150 (wiki: N, UCM speaker-only).

question: Which microphones does surya have, and on which inputs?
found: Two built-in analog microphones on the WCD9375: the bottom one on AMIC1 (mic bias 1) into ADC1, the top one on AMIC3 (mic bias 3) into ADC2 with its input mux at INP3; the headset mic is AMIC2 (bias 2) on the same ADC2 at INP2. ADC1 comes back over the TX SoundWire bus on master port 2, ADC2 needs its own master port 3 (qcom,tx-port-mapping <2 3 4 5>): sharing port 2 with ADC1 lost the top mic and turned the bottom one to full-scale noise (pulpoff). No digital mics: pulpoff names LPI gpio7-11 NC, among them gpio8-11, the DMIC clock and data pins (vendor gpio26-29), and records both mics through ADC1/ADC2 on mainline. The TX DMIC1-3 routes read on 2026-11-17 come from sdmmagpie-qrd-overlay.dts, Qualcomm's QRD reference board kept in Xiaomi's tree, which declares the SWR_ADC0/ADC2 routes beside them. Measured on the phone (bring-up, 2026-11-17 04:37 UTC, test/surya-mic with <&swr2 1>): mic-records pass and mic-hears-speaker pass, a 1 kHz tone at -19.4 dBFS against -76.3 dBFS of noise through ADC1. The DMIC experiment (pins at mux 1, VA DMIC clocks on a switch) answered a question surya does not ask and is to be dropped.

question: Which public number can an automated call reach from a German mobile, that plays back what it hears, free or at the national rate?
found: Only one German public echo line is attested across sources and years: blueSIP's echo test, +49 89 721010 99701, a Munich landline number (landline rate: inside any German allnet flat, about 9 ct/min on plain prepaid), named in forums in 2005 and 2013, recommended in 2021, and still on Placetel's list (which gives no warranty). It plays back what it hears at once (an echo, not record-then-playback); no length limit is stated. The same provider's +49 89 721010 99702 plays a signal tone: a downlink-only control that needs no working uplink. sipgate's echo (10005) and test (10000) are SIP-internal short codes, not dialable from a mobile, and sipgate serves only business customers since 2025-06. Other European lines (portunity's 0211 237099929 from 2005, sip2sip's +31 20 8005161, a Dutch C*NET echo) are old and unconfirmed, and abroad costs more. No source confirms any line works from a mobile today, so the first supervised call settles it. Fallback that is certain to exist and free on German tariffs: the SIM's own mailbox (record a message, play it back by DTMF; slower and operator-specific).

question: How can the phone itself decide that a call carried sound both ways?
found: Acoustically, through the paths a person uses, with the analysis in Rust: during the call the uplink capture that the call needs anyway (1 channel on TX_CODEC_DMA_TX_3, the bottom mic) is written to a file instead of thrown away. The phone plays a pattern of three short tones (e.g. 800, 1300, 1900 Hz, 200 ms each, 300 ms apart - inside the 300-3400 Hz every voice codec keeps) on the loudspeaker at the manifest's quiet level; the bottom mic hears it at once (proves the injection) and sends it up the call; the echo comes back down and plays on the earpiece, and the same mic hears it again 150-1500 ms later (the network's round trip; acoustic reflections are under 20 ms). A Goertzel envelope per frequency finds the pattern twice; the echo counts when the same order of tones recurs at one delay, 15 dB above the noise, and the delay is reported. Before the echo call, a call to the tone line (99702) proves the downlink alone, so a missing echo says uplink (or the line) rather than everything. Cost: one call of at most 25 s (dial, about 8 s to answer, 5 s of pattern, hang up; a hard timeout), at most once a day, a landline-rate number: inside a flat, or under 10 ct per day on prepaid. Skips cleanly, as unknown: no modem, no SIM, not registered, no voice interface, no call path (call-audio-path failing), the daily call already made, or the number unset in the manifest. A pass proves works for modem-calls. If q6voice exposes in-call record/playback ports (downstream's VOICE_RECORD_RX, incall music), a digital loop could replace the acoustic one later; unknown on this driver.

question: How should the phones' health suites be organised to cover every part and feature, stay quick to change and dependable, and avoid Python?
found: What is: devlab-health, a static Rust runner (lab-tools/health), runs shell checks on the phone after every boot in two layers (base, shell): 11 generic in lab-tools and 5 of surya's own in surya-lab; each prints 'pass|fail|skip TEST COMPONENT detail' and docs' tests table says what each pass proves. The weak spot is computation in shell: three of surya's checks carry a Goertzel filter written in awk and a tone made byte by byte with printf, because lab-tools' tested tone crate never reaches the phone. The phone has no Rust toolchain (it has python3, which the lab refuses), so rust-script (stable, 0.36 on the lab) cannot run there and would need a toolchain and network on the phone; Cargo's own single-file scripts (frontmatter, cargo PR 16569) are still nightly-only in Cargo 1.99. KTAP is the kernel's test output (ok/not ok, SKIP, nested suites) - a format our lines map onto if LAVA-style tools are ever wanted. Shape that fits: shell stays for what is a reading (sysfs, a command's output; ten readable lines), and anything with numbers, timing or a state machine (tones, echoes, calls, sleep counters) is a subcommand of one static multi-call Rust binary shipped with devlab-health (e.g. devlab-health tone find, devlab-health call echo), built with its unit tests and recorded fixtures on the lab and cross-built by health/build.sh; rust-script is the lab's prototyping and one-off analysis tool against recordings fetched from the phone, a prototype becoming a subcommand once it is kept. Coverage is read off the data: a query of every device's components with no test that proves works, and a layer per cost - base, shell, then telephony (calls and data, gated by budget and once a day) and witnessed (needs a person).

question: How can mobile data be checked after every boot within about 3 GB?
found: Per run: the modem registered and its bearer connected (mmcli), the bearer's interface found from ModemManager, then over that interface only (curl --interface, so Wi-Fi cannot pass for it): a DNS lookup, five pings to a fixed address (round trip, loss), and a 100 kB HTTPS download timed (speed.cloudflare.com/__down?bytes=100000 or a file the project hosts), about 150 kB with overheads. Boots run up to ~45 a day in bring-up, so about 7 MB on a heavy day; once a week a 5 MB download measures throughput. That is under 0.3 GB a month even on busy months: the 3 GB lasts most of a year at the worst rate and years at an ordinary one. A check also reads the bearer's own byte counters (the interface's /sys/class/net/IFACE/statistics before and after) so each run states what it used, and skips when the month's total passes a budget set in the manifest. Skips without a SIM, as the modem checks already do.

question: Should linux-phone-oco keep standing expert sessions, one per hard domain (audio, modem, sleep...), with the orchestrator routing questions to them - or keep expertise somewhere else?
found: The world has tried it under several names - specialised workers under a supervisor, hierarchical teams, blackboard systems, stateful agents - and converges on one split: the expert is a role and a body of written knowledge; a session is a disposable worker that takes the role up. Gas Town says it outright (an agent is a persistent identity, sessions are cattle; any session can hand off and restart from its hook). Anthropic's long-running harness found compaction alone not enough and had every fresh session get up to speed from a progress file, git and a feature list; its context-engineering guide names notes outside the window as the tool for iterative work with milestones. Claude Code itself moved this way: subagents may keep a per-role MEMORY.md, and agent teams start each teammate from project context and a spawn prompt, never the lead's history, and do not restore teammates on resume. Against expertise held in a long context: models recall worse as input grows (Chroma, context rot; Anthropic's attention budget), repeated summarising erodes detail (ACE: context collapse, brevity bias), and a session of 1000-1800 messages re-reads all of it each turn - after an idle hour without the cache, at full price - so a standing expert answering an occasional question is the costliest and not the most reliable way to answer it. Against a central router: a supervisor that relays every message plays telephone - lower scores and more tokens than agents handing off directly (LangChain); misalignment between agents (lost context, withheld information) is one of the three failure groups in 1600 traces (MAST). What works (Cognition, 2026): one writer per thing, other agents adding intelligence not actions; a consult works best given a fork of the asker's full context. Blackboard systems route by a shared record agents read, not by a relay. For us: most of the audio expertise is already rows in docs (5 research, 2 decisions, 27 backlog items name the microphone); what is not written is the tacit part - dead ends, where the experiment patches are, what hung the phone - and it now lives in hand-over notes outside any repository.

question: How do open practice and agent makers organise a knowledge base so that people and agents reach what they need without reading all of it?
found: They agree. (1) One small entry that is always read and routes onward, saying what each target is for: llms.txt, the root AGENTS.md (nearest wins), PhotoCraft's Read/Why orientation table, Johnny.Decimal's index, datapackage.json. (2) What is always loaded is kept small: CLAUDE.md under 200 lines, no more than ten per level, llms.txt's skippable Optional. (3) Detail in stages: Skills' name and line, then body, then linked files; Claude Code loads nested CLAUDE.md only when its subtree is touched; context engineering keeps lightweight identifiers - paths, stored queries - and loads content just in time. (4) Small units with stable addresses: evergreen notes whose titles work like APIs, numbered ADRs, Wikidata's Q and P ids. (5) Facts apart from explanation: Diátaxis' reference against explanation, Wikidata statements and infoboxes beside prose. (6) One decision per record, superseded rather than deleted (Nygard, MADR). (7) Every statement is about an item by its id and cites who says so (Wikidata). (8) Views are generated from the source data (PhotoCraft's scorecard, Mintlify's llms.txt). Tensions: hierarchy against association (fixed buckets vs dense links - a small fixed index with free links beneath answers both); one file against many (concatenation does not save context; loading on demand does). No source measured how much any of it speeds an agent - the measure here is docs' own (kb-navigation-measured).

question: What in the commons already does part of an ideal knowledge base, and would idealkb be one nature under a second name?
found: tad (creation-guidelines/tad-engine) is the engine: tables declared as data after Frictionless Table Schema, checked rows, canonical files, SQL, named queries and records with their header line as their description (tad statements is already an index of every question and record a base keeps). text-as-data-template is the template for a base kept as tad data - the same nature as idealkb - and has drifted: last changed 2026-11-04, still the vendored Python engine on a DuckDB schema that every base left on 2026-11-11 (as the vendored engines had drifted, three of four behind). ideal-project-playbook is how to run a software project - the loop, guards, CI, honesty - whose own docs/ is a tad base; its kit/templates for backlog, development log and idea page are records a base keeps as tables, and its findability test (real questions, the answer within the first three) is the measure a base needs. software-engineering-canon is a base itself (the spike the template came from). ideal-agent (grenudi/ideal-agent, 2026-11-17) is how agents work: practices, skills, hooks, and its own tad base; it keeps only what is general and leaves a project's domain in the project's data. ocoeco's marks (oco.toml exports, holds) and lenses say how a base fits the observatory's picture - its face, not its organisation. linux-phone-oco/docs is one tad base for every linux-phone place (2026-11-17-one-database), with prompts/ (role briefs), research/ (long prose), and rendered docs/ the face reads. Overlap: idealkb would be text-as-data-template under a second name; nothing else holds how knowledge is organised. Gap: no base links a record to what it is about, and no base has an entry that routes questions to queries.

(3) Mainline Linux: no Pixel 2 device tree; arm64/qcom has MSM8998 boards (OnePlus 5/5T, Xiaomi Mi 6, Sony yoshino, F(x)tec Pro1, HP Envy x2, Lenovo Miix 630, Asus NovaGo) and msm8998.dtsi was still edited on 2026-09-17. (4) The port lives out of tree: kcxt/linux-wahoo, created 2020-07-20, last pushed 2022-02-27; branch wahoo/5.17 has msm8998-google-taimen.dts, -walleye.dts and wahoo.dtsi, plus panel and DPU/DSC work (unfinished), and a taimen-5.11-submit branch whose mainline submission is not found upstream. Not found for either: Mobian, Droidian, Sailfish, a pmOS issue or MR (search only; absence is not a report). SoC and surya: MSM8998 (Snapdragon 835, 2017) vs SM7150 (Snapdragon 732G). Sibling evidence for the SoC: the wiki's OnePlus 5 (archived, kernel field 6.0) reports touch, screen, wifi, Bluetooth, 3D, GPS Y and audio, mobile data, calls, SMS, sensors N: a different phone, stale, context only. Distance: surya has 12 of 20 parts working by its own tests; the Pixel 2 XL has 1 community 'works' (flashing), 1 'broken' (screen) and 19 unknown; the Pixel 2 has nothing reported.

question: What must a phone have, structurally, to be a daily driver - judged from everything the open and proprietary platforms already built, learned and failed at?
found: Nine structural concepts, from ten projects, two operating systems and one firmware: Two Minds (a small always-on processor beside the main one, proven by Crust), Radio Wall, Notification Sovereignty, Consolidation Path, Platform Compatibility, Security Substrate, Update Covenant, Power Covenant, and the Observatory that maps every project against them. The open ecosystem's hard gaps are standby with push, a hardware security processor and long-term updates; Android and iOS solved them in closed ways. The model, its map and the prior-art files for Android/AOSP, iOS and GrapheneOS are the material; it is the why layer of the grand picture. (Moved into the dated layout on 2026-11-17.)

brief: Phone tests are small executables printing one line per case; nobody compiles on the device; upstream pmOS covers only initramfs tests today, so we keep their shape and own the runner
question: How are tests organised, shipped and provisioned on Linux phones (postmarketOS, bootrr, LAVA, CI-tron, systemd), where do rust-script tests plus a bundle crate fit, and should we build fully on postmarketOS upstream?
found: postmarketOS (postmarketos-test subpackages, initramfs hook), bootrr, LAVA and CI-tron share one shape: a test is a small executable, a thin runner prints one pass/fail/skip line per case, the lab collects the lines, device facts live as data. Nobody compiles on the device. rust-script compiles on first run and needs rust+cargo on the phone (Alpine aarch64: 72 MiB download, 206 MiB installed plus gcc/musl-dev/llvm-libs, network for crates): fine on the lab, poor on a phone. A bundle crate that depends on tests (nextest discovery, inventory/linkme) is sound as design but unproven on aarch64 musl; one binary per test found by directory gives the same independence. Provisioning: an apk gives versions, uninstall and signatures at the price of a key and a repository (ours is published); a lab push is fast and leaves no version record. UPSTREAM (checked 2026-11-17; their sites now redirect to nura.eco): MRs on their GitLab with Alpine-style commit rules and approval rules; on-device tests are postmarketos-test-* subpackages run by an initramfs hook that halts the boot; only kernel/initramfs tests work today, boot and system tests (modem, Wi-Fi, audio, sleep - what we need) are not built; their farm is a CI-tron gateway with one OnePlus 6T, joining is token-gated and undocumented; Python is host-side only (pipeline generation, pmbootstrap) and costs nothing on the phone. Whether rhizcuts handle a GitLab subfolder is not known. Weighed: fully upstream (A), our runner with upstreamable shell files in their shape (B), a different shape (C). Chosen B. Not known yet: pmaports licence/CLA, fork-sync cost, bootrr contribution policy, rust-script cache path, inventory/linkme on aarch64 musl, the systemd claims (memory only).

brief: What the vendor's GPL kernel says walleye's hardware is: Samsung S6E3FA5 panel, Synaptics touch, WCD934x + TAS2557, DRV2624, PMI8998 charger and gauge, NQ NFC, WCN3990, sensors behind the SLPI
question: Which chip is each part of the Pixel 2 (walleye) and how is it wired, by Google's GPL wahoo kernel device tree and the mainline port's tree?
found:
Read from the LineageOS copy of Google's wahoo kernel (4.4, branch lineage-22.2) and kcxt/linux-wahoo wahoo/5.17; observed facts only, nothing copied; table in research/google-walleye/2026-11-17/vendor-kernel-hardware-inventory.md.
Walleye is the HTC-built half of the pair: its files are under dts/htc/ and called "muskie"; one base plus one of two overlays by board revision (xa/xb/xc or xd/xe/a; our MP1 maps to one of them - not known yet). SoC MSM8998 v2.1 with PM8998, PMI8998 and PM8005.
Parts: panel Samsung S6E3FA5 5.0 in 1080x1920 command mode, 4 DSI lanes, reset GPIO94, TE GPIO10, rails PM8998 L14 1.8 V and L22 3.0 V, backlight by DCS (no WLED), always-on modes. Touch Synaptics DSX at I2C 0x20 on the BLSP1 QUP5 bus (GPIO87/88), IRQ GPIO125, reset GPIO89. Audio: WCD934x "Tavil" codec on SLIMbus, TI TAS2557 stereo speaker amp at I2C 0x4d, no jack; NXP TFA98xx amps are in the tree but disabled. Haptics TI DRV2624 (LRA 155 Hz, I2C 0x5a, reset GPIO95). LED: TI LP5562 on early revisions, PMI8998 RGB on later. Charger: PMI8998 SMB2 with Type-C PD, TPS61099 for USB host power, NXP PTN36241G redriver. Fuel gauge: PMI8998 FG gen3 with HTC battery module, 2700 mAh, 4.4 V. NFC: NXP NQ-class at 0x28 plus PN81A secure element on SPI. Fingerprint FPC1020 family (IRQ GPIO86, reset GPIO128). Wi-Fi and Bluetooth: Qualcomm WCN3990 (Bluetooth HCI on BLSP1 UART3). Cameras: two CCI sensors, rear with autofocus, OIS, EEPROM and flash, laser ranger at I2C 0x29; the sensor chips are not named in the tree (public specs: Sony IMX362 rear, IMX179 front). Pixel Visual Core ("Easel") on PCIe 0 with a BCM15602 PMIC and SPI. Storage UFS. Sensors (IMU, magnetometer, barometer, light, Hall) are not in the application processor's tree: the SLPI sensor-hub DSP owns them, firmware proprietary.
For a phone with no display: stock describes a RAM console (ramoops) at 0xa1100000, 2 MiB, plus an alternate at 0xa3800000; the mainline port uses 0xa1810000 instead and boots with console on ttyMSM1 (BLSP2 UART1) and a USB-gadget serial ttyGS0 - which address survives a reset on this phone is not known yet.
The mainline port's walleye file is 13 lines and sets no panel (the shared file's panel is taimen's LG one), and enables UFS, USB peripheral, one DSI, GPU, Wi-Fi, SLPI and ADSP, regulators - nothing for touch, audio, haptics, NFC, gauge, charger, cameras, sensors.
Not known yet: camera and sensor chips on walleye itself, touch controller model, codec exact part, fingerprint wiring, Active Edge sensing, UART test pads, which overlay MP1 uses.

brief: Only taimen reached a shell on mainline (USB gadget console, black screen, a special dtbo); walleye has a tree nobody reports booting; a USB-C UART cable is tested on walleye
question: How did others boot Linux on the Pixel 2 family (boot image, A/B, fastboot boot, dtbo), what boots, and how did they reach a phone with no display?
found:
Only the Pixel 2 XL (taimen) is reported to have booted mainline, by kcxt (Caleb Connolly) on an out-of-tree 5.10 to 5.17 fork, 2020 to 2022: black screen, USB networking to a shell, flashing works; a March 2021 mainline submission shows no sign of being merged. Walleye has a 13-line tree in the same fork and no report that it boots; neither phone is in pmaports (Pixel 3, 3 XL, 3a are). Ubuntu Touch (Halium 9, Android 4.4 kernel) has only an abandoned 16.04 port for walleye, with boot loops and no USB networking in the forum threads read.
How the no-display phone was reached: USB peripheral mode only (SuperSpeed dropped), kernel console on a USB serial gadget ttyGS0 plus ttyMSM1 earlycon, clk_ignore_unused; a UART through the USB-C sideband pins ('Android Debug Cable', 115200 baud) which the pmOS wiki lists as tested with walleye - enabled with `fastboot oem uart enable`; pstore only partly worked. What the bootloader wants (XL only, read): a dtbo partition holding an overlay with id 2704 (0xa90) or the bootloader refuses to boot; pmaports' Pixel 3 packages append the dtb to the kernel (4096-byte pages, kernel offset 0x8000, ramdisk 0x1000000), LineageOS uses Image.lz4-dtb with recovery in the boot partition and A/B, 8 MB dtbo. Detail and URLs in research/google-walleye/2026-11-17/how-others-booted-wahoo.md.
Not known yet: whether this phone's bootloader accepts `fastboot boot` of our image; the dtbo id walleye needs (the README is XL only; changing dtbo writes to the phone); whether `fastboot oem uart enable` only sets a RAM flag or writes something (until known, it is a change to the phone); the boot header version; slot handling for a Linux boot; any report for the small Pixel 2 booting mainline.
Ways forward: (1) read walleye's dtbo overlay ids without writing (from Android if it boots, or Google's factory image, a proprietary download - decision needed); (2) try a first `fastboot boot` of a kernel with appended dtb and a USB-gadget serial console once devlab's fastboot mode exists; (3) build the USB-C debug cable and enable the UART only after a decision on the oem command.

brief: First boot: v0 boot.img, dtb appended with qcom,msm-id, no bootargs in the dts, USB 2.0 gadget instead of a display; whether fastboot boot works with a mainline dtb and the dtbo is not known
question: What does a first mainline boot of the Pixel 2 need, and what can and cannot fastboot boot do on this bootloader?
found:
Image: boot header v0, base 0x0, kernel offset 0x8000, ramdisk 0x1000000, tags 0x100, page 4096 - verified by porthole against the stock TAIMEN boot.img; LineageOS's wahoo board config says tags 0x01E00000 / ramdisk 0x02000000 instead: two sets are reported, walleye's own stock boot.img header decides (not read yet). Boot partition is 32 MiB (getvar boot_a 0x2000000), max-download-size 0x20000000: size is no limit. The DTB is appended to the kernel; it must carry qcom,msm-id = <0x124 0x20001> (taimen has it, kcxt's walleye does not).
Cmdline (porthole): clk_ignore_unused ignore_loglevel panic=10 earlycon=msm_serial_dm,0xc1b0000 qcom_wdt.arm_on_probe=1 watchdog.open_timeout=300 reboot=w; kcxt adds console=ttyGS0,115200. No bootargs/stdout-path in the DTS: ABL appends the boot.img cmdline with fdt_appendprop_string, and a pre-existing bootargs hides it.
Display: command-mode panels, so no scanned-out framebuffer for simple-framebuffer; the first sign of life must be USB. Path: dwc3 peripheral, high-speed only, SuperSpeed PHY dropped, qcom,select-utmi-as-pipe-clk, assigned-clock-rates 19.2/60 MHz (works on taimen); initramfs with a configfs gadget (ACM console + RNDIS/ECM) and telnet/ssh on 172.16.42.1 (devlab's address). pstore: ramoops 0xa1810000/0x200000; a cold reset scrambles it, so the warm-reset/watchdog parameters matter. UART: the Pixel debug cable (see google-walleye-how-others-booted; fastboot oem uart enable is a change to the phone, undecided).
Bootloader (keeper's read-only getvar, google-walleye-bootloader-first-look): mw8998-003.0085.00, hw-revision MP1, unlocked, A/B both slots successful, avb_version 1.0.0, kernel:uefi, no fastbootd.
fastboot boot: TWRP's own instructions for walleye use it (xdaforums), but another report could not boot TWRP that way, and nobody reports a mainline kernel booted from RAM on any Pixel 2: NOT known. Also not known: whether ABL applies the stock dtbo of the active slot to a mainline DTB (taimen's bootloader refuses a kernel unless dtbo holds overlay id 2704 - kcxt's README, taimen only; porthole flashes its own stub into slot b), and what vbmeta/AVB does to an unsigned image on an unlocked phone. One try through devlab (walleye-first-fastboot-boot) answers all three; a refusal is an answer, and the stub dtbo is a write (the author's decision; backlog walleye-dtbo-overlay-id).

brief: Clean room with agents works as an input wall (observer, scrubber, implementer, spec rows with evidence); walleye needs it for few MSM8998 parts; GPL vendor source needs none
question: How is clean-room reverse engineering best done with AI agents, and how should walleye's bring-up apply it?
found: Agents are now near-human at reading binaries (arXiv 2610.14960; 2608.11469 SRE-Bench: best agents solve ~27-32% of realistic ones), but no paper yet covers clean-room hardware bring-up; the practice does. AI "clean rooms" (ArtCraft: a rule on inputs; chardet 7.0: disputed) cannot prove the wall by the model's mind, only by what it was shown - so use an INPUT wall: observer (traces on the stock system, GPL vendor kernel source, public specs) writes spec rows with evidence kind + hash; a separate scrubber checks them for expression; the implementer sees only accepted rows, public specs and mainline; commits cite spec ids; per-session input log and taint register. Tools: mmiotrace/ftrace/dynamic debug/regmap/QMI logs/debugfs on the running stock system (Nouveau, Asahi m1n1 tracing, freedreno), never disassembly or vendor binaries (Asahi: 'without looking at the code'). Walleye: most MSM8998 parts are upstream and need no clean room; likely only panel init, sensor hub, audio calibration/topology, camera, vendor protocols. brief: Pixel 2 Load Error: format matches what Pixel 3 ABL accepts; likely causes are the dtbo overlay merge, missing board-id/pmic-id, slot state, the os word - a control image first
question: What does the Pixel 2 bootloader dislike in our boot images (Load Error), from public sources, and which variants should be tried next?
found:
What is: four images, one kernel/dtb/initramfs, all v0 with the dtb appended to a gzipped Image (Image.gz+dtb). a (taimen offsets, os word 0) got "Booting OKAY" then silence; b (LineageOS offsets) first left fastboot (Android came back on slot b), later Load Error; c and d (a, b plus os_version 8.1.0 / patch 2020-01) both Load Error. The only difference between a and c is that header word.

What others show (not the Pixel 2 itself - nobody reports a mainline fastboot boot there):
1. The format is the accepted one. Stock ABL on the same line (Pixel 3) takes a gzipped kernel with the dtb appended in a v0 boot image (U-Boot's board doc), and postmarketOS boots blueline with exactly base 0 / kernel 0x8000 / ramdisk 0x1000000 / tags 0x100 / page 4096 / dtb appended (pmaports deviceinfo). Two differences from our images: pmaports sets second offset 0 (we use 0xf00000; second is empty, so it should not matter) and no os_version/patch level at all. So "header v0 vs what ABL expects" and "Image.gz-dtb vs Image+dtb" are not the likely cause; the os word is, if anything, the one thing we added that pmaports does not have.
2. ABL, not the kernel, picks and patches the dtb (Inoki, MSM8998 Nokia 8): DeviceTreeAppended scans the appended blobs and DeviceTreeCompatible matches qcom,msm-id, qcom,board-id and qcom,pmic-id. Our dts carries only msm-id (0x124 0x20001, as kcxt's taimen, which boots with msm-id alone); it has no board-id or pmic-id. Whether walleye's ABL accepts that is not known; the stock walleye dtb's ids are not read yet (not in the public sources reached today).
3. The bootloader merges a dtbo overlay into the dtb before the kernel starts (AOSP DTO). kcxt found the taimen bootloader refuses a mainline kernel unless the dtbo partition holds an overlay with id 2704, and flashes a stub. Stock overlays patch downstream nodes a mainline base does not have, so a failed merge is the best-fitting reading of an immediate "Load Error" that comes from the bootloader after the transfer. Not proven for walleye: the dtbo of slot b is an older LineageOS build's, its overlay table not read.
4. "Load Error" is not proof the image is bad. Known-good TWRP for walleye got the same words from fastboot boot (Android SE), and one XDA report says it appeared randomly and went away on restart. Our slot flags (a unbootable, current b) were left by the first try; whether they feed the refusal is not known.
5. "Booting OKAY" then silence (a) means the bootloader sent its OK and a later step failed or the kernel died before any sign of life; it is a different outcome from Load Error, and a is the only image that got it. The os word turning OKAY into Load Error says the refusal is sensitive to the header word - the likeliest reason is the bootloader comparing the os_version/patch level with the active slot's recorded one (not read anywhere; unknown).

Ranked causes (each has a try that tells it apart): (H1) overlay merge fails against a mainline base, so a stub dtbo or a dtb that survives the stock overlay is needed - only fixable by a write (dtbo_b stub) or by finding that slot b's dtbo is not the cause; (H2) dtb ids: msm-id only, no board-id/pmic-id; free to test on the host; (H3) state: slot flags or random Load Error; test with a control image; (H4) header word: only os word 0 passes, so keep 0.
Control first: a stock-format image known to boot on walleye (LineageOS or TWRP recovery for walleye, public) through the same fastboot boot path. If the control also gets Load Error, the cause is the phone's state and no image change helps; if it boots, the cause is in our image and the variants below tell which part. The control is a try, not a write.
Not read yet and worth reading without writing: walleye's stock boot.img header and dtb ids from a public LineageOS wahoo build (host only), slot b's dtbo overlay ids (pstore/Android adb read - keeper only).

brief: No tool does build, swap and check of a boot image in Rust; the parts exist (header, cpio, dtb, compression) and the oracles are mkbootimg and avbtool, so we wrap.
question: What exists to build, unpack, swap and check Android boot images and initramfs for a phone bring-up, and what does walleye's shell do today?
found:
What is: walleye's bring-up is 8 POSIX shell scripts (~520 lines) in google-walleye-lab/build plus tests/host/gadget-up.sh; they call mkbootimg, unpack_bootimg and avbtool (Python from android-tools), the kernel's gen_init_cpio, lz4, fdtget/fdtdump, with their own checks (check-bootimg, check-bisect count fields and fail). Their knowledge is worth keeping: header v0 offsets by variant, the appended dtb, the lz4 frame shape of the stock kernel, the AVB hash footer (algorithm NONE, padded to the control's size), the NET=43 address rewrite, xz because the 4.4 kernel has no gzip. surya's bring-up had no scripts (by hand). Earlier records already decided the family: backlog rust-toolset (one Rust toolset in lab-tools, rust-script for small scripts, pmbootstrap read as reference) and decision 2026-11-17-health-checks-shell-and-rust (shell for plain readings, Rust for logic, rust-script for prototypes and one-offs).
Others: nothing covers the whole job. Android's mkbootimg/unpack_bootimg/repack_bootimg and avbtool (Python) are the authoritative oracles; magiskboot (Rust+C++, GPL) has the model of swapping one part (unpack to a directory, change, repack with the original as template) but is aimed at rooting; abootimg-oxide 0.5.2 (Rust, MIT/Apache, 2026-06) reads and writes header v0-v4 and vendor_boot; abootcrafter has an update flow, no AVB; abl-exorcist (Rust, GPL) shells out to mkbootimg; no AVB crate exists on crates.io (avbroot, GPL, does vbmeta, is no library). Rust crates for the rest: cpio 0.4.2 (newc writer), flate2, lz4_flex (maintained), dtoolkit 0.5.0 (Google, dtb read/edit, young), fdt (read). pmbootstrap is Python, ~24k lines in 129 files; its deviceinfo names (header_version, base, kernel_offset, ramdisk_offset, tags_offset, pagesize, cmdline) are the vocabulary to reuse; the boot image is not built there. Mobian, Droidian (initramfs-tools-halium: shell hooks for an initramfs only), lk2nd (a bootloader, no host tooling): nothing to take. No tool checks an image against expected header fields; unpack_bootimg plus a comparison is all there is, which is what our check scripts do.
Not known yet: whether abootimg-oxide writes byte-identical v0 images; dtoolkit's maturity; whether cpio 0.4.2 reads; whether boot-deploy, Mobian and Halium scripts add anything (not read; the outside look was done by a read-only researcher from page summaries, so counts are weaker than a source read).
Where tools live today: lab-tools (its README: tools for bringing up and testing Linux phones, not tied to one device) is the one place already: devlab (the phone: fastboot, flash, kernel try, provision, keeper, health, MCP; 5.4k lines with rmcp and tokio), health (runs on the phone) and tone. Device repos hold data and thin scripts.

brief: A tool is followed by a pin, not files: device parts live beside it as data, hooks or a rust-script on the pinned library; rhizoid carries the cutting and slice cases and lacks three things.
question: How do device repositories use, extend, send back to and update from a tools home, side by side with no rebase, and where does rhizoid fit?
found:
The question: a home for bring-up tools must also let device repositories use them, extend them with device-specific parts, send useful changes back and pull updates in, their own changes side by side with no rebase each time (the author's words, relayed by the coordinator; the problem git-rhizoid was started for). Extends research bringup-tools-landscape.
What is: the chain already decided (idealkb decision 2026-11-17-chain-follow-by-slice, research chain-follow-world): one pin-and-follow mechanism for data and briefs - a source names its generic files, a follower pins a release and keeps its own files, a changed generic file ends follow.sh with exit 3 and goes back as an upstream item (ikb upstream-item, form patch), weekly update-pins and a release gate; device bases follow idealkb and device-template that way. It lays a slice of files. Rhizoid (git-rhizoid.github.io, rhizoid repo) is for whole forks: a cutting is a fork owned and pinned, tracking branch pristine, patch branch merged from it, rhizoid's own metadata additive-only, so a diff of patch against tracking is a clean patch back; its CLI is typed but add/update/status are stubbed, its consumption side is open (design-consumption-side) and slice-consumption was added 2026-11-17 by the idealkb chain. devlab and lpoco-health already reach consumers as released packages (release-plz tags, the packaging conveyor), not as copied files.
Finding: a tool is not a slice. Compiled logic is followed by a version pin, not by files laid into the follower, so the rebase trouble does not arise for the tool at all as long as a device never edits the tool's tree: its own parts live in its own repository, beside the tool, in three levels. (1) Data: device.toml [boot] and the files it names (initramfs skeleton, dtb variants). (2) Hooks: executables the manifest names for a step (shell where stupid simple), called with the paths in arguments, a nonzero exit stops the job. (3) Logic: a rust-script file (or a small crate) in the device repository whose header depends on bringup's library at the pinned tag (rust-script and cargo take a git tag as a dependency). Only two things then need the follow machinery: the pin (a version line the follower owns) and the slice of files that go with the tool in device-template (the [boot] skeleton, hook examples). Sending back: a generic improvement is a pull request to lab-tools from the device's branch, recorded in the device base as an upstream item (form patch) against a lab-tools upstream row seeded beside idealkb and device-template; an update comes by a pin bump (the weekly job, a pull request per source). Side by side: the device's changes are files of its own, so a pin bump touches none of them; when a device must patch the tool itself before upstream takes it, that is a cutting of lab-tools consumed as a git dependency (Cargo [patch]) - rhizoid's exact case, rare because the three levels cover most.
Where rhizoid carries it, and what it lacks (recorded on its own backlog, git-rhizoid.github.io PR 28, not worked around): a cutting consumed by a language manager - writing and bumping the pin where cargo or rust-script reads it (cutting-as-cargo-dependency); one pin file, one bump, one verdict for slices, cuttings and tool versions together (followers-one-pin-bump); sending a patch back as a pull request on the person's word with the follower's own record of it (send-back-writes-the-upstream-item); and slice-consumption (already open) for the template files. Until rhizoid has them: idealkb's follow.sh and update-pins for the slices, a plain fork with a [patch] line for the rare cutting, recorded as a problem.
Not known yet: whether bringup's library API can stay stable enough for the third level while it is 0.x (the first builder's test of pin refusal tells); whether a host binary release (asset) or cargo install --git is the simpler install for a device lab (bringup-release settles it).

question: Should linux-phone-oco's tools share one prefix (lpoco-bringup, lpoco-health; devlab, tone renamed or not), or none?
found:
What is: lab-tools has devlab (host command, built from the clone, named in about 450 files of linux-phone-oco and in the MCP door's tool names), tone (a library crate and its command, not installed anywhere) and lpoco-health (a package shipped to phones, renamed from devlab-health when it became one, the old name kept as another name). Collisions checked 2026-11-17: crates.io already has a crate named tone (0.0.1); devlab, bringup and lpoco-bringup are not taken as crates, none is on the lab's PATH or in the Arch repositories.
How others do it: git-* and cargo-* are discovered by the prefix itself (a subcommand is any git-NAME or cargo-NAME on PATH) and complete at the prompt; pmbootstrap and pmaports carry pm for postmarketOS across the whole family; systemd uses a suffix (*ctl) for the same purpose. In each, the prefix marks the tools others install, and it names whose they are.
Finding: share the prefix where the tool is installed or pinned by others (lpoco-health, lpoco-bringup); keep the short names of the lab's own commands (devlab, tone) until they are installed elsewhere - renaming them now costs about 450 references, the installed path and the MCP tool names for no reader's gain, and the alias precedent (devlab-health kept as another name) makes the later rename cheap. A mixed family is acceptable when the rule is one sentence. Not known yet: when devlab is first pinned by a device repository (that triggers its rename).

brief: One roof: an lpoco dispatcher (git-style) runs lpoco-NAME programs, one pin, one release, one MCP door; each tool stays its own small crate; old names stay as aliases.
question: Should all lpoco tools sit under one command, one pin and one release (the author: one roof), and in what form?
found: Asked by the author after the prefix amendment: the point was to gather all tools of lpoco under one roof. Forms: (a) one lpoco command with subcommands, as git and cargo do - a dispatcher that runs lpoco-NAME found beside it or on PATH; (b) every tool renamed lpoco-* now, released together; (c) the prefix rule with devlab and tone deferred (the first amendment). What a roof buys: one install, one pin in device.toml [tools], one completion and man page, one MCP server, one place agents look. What it costs: ~450 references to devlab and the MCP tool names, softened by keeping the old names as other names (the lpoco-health precedent). Constraint: lpoco-health ships to phones as a small static binary (opt-level s, no tokio, no rmcp), so a single fat binary would grow the phone's program; a dispatcher keeps every tool its own crate and binary, testable and runnable alone. Finding: (a) as a dispatcher over lpoco-* programs, family released together with a version lockstep check, the new tool born as lpoco-bringup under it; devlab becomes lpoco lab (devlab kept as another name), tone lpoco tone, the MCP door becomes lpoco mcp. Not known yet: whether release-plz makes one family tag easily (the builder of lpoco-dispatcher settles it); whether a feature-gated single binary would later be simpler.

brief: abootimg-oxide 0.5.2 writes the v0 header byte for byte as mkbootimg; the id (SHA-1 of three parts) and trailing padding are the caller's
question: Does abootimg-oxide write header v0 byte-exact, or must pack wrap mkbootimg?
found: Measured 2026-11-17 with a scratch program against mkbootimg (android-tools, header v0, base 0, kernel 0x8000, ramdisk 0x1000000, tags 0x100, page 4096): the crate's header write gave bytes identical to mkbootimg for the whole length it wrote. Two gaps, both ours to fill: (1) full_write only seeks to boot_image_size, so the image ends before the last page's padding (15288 of 16384 bytes) - pack pads itself; (2) the header id: mkbootimg's v0 id is SHA-1 over kernel, ramdisk and second, each followed by its u32 size (three parts), while the crate's compute_hash_digest hashes five (adds recovery dtbo and dtb) - so for v0 the id is computed in our code. With both, pack equals mkbootimg for the plain header and with os_version/os_patch_level words (tests/pack_v0.rs, two cases). mkbootimg writes second address 0 when there is no second image, whatever second_offset says. Header::parse reads v0..v2 and v3/v4; this tool reads v0 only for now. Cost: binrw and thiserror come with the crate. Not known yet: v1/v2 write parity, vendor_boot.

brief: The lab host is prepared by hand today (udev, modules, toolchain, watchers, host tools); nobody derives host rules from device declarations; uaccess reaches only the seat's active session
question: How does the lab host get prepared for the devices it serves, from each device repository's device.toml, by a tool under the lpoco roof, with no manual step outside a tool - and how do others do it?
found:
INSIDE. Nothing prepares the lab host from declarations today; each part got there by hand or by a one-machine script. Measured read-only on the lab (grig, systemd 262): the lab user (uid 1000) is in neither disk (/dev/sdX) nor uucp (/dev/ttyACM* on Arch), so walleye's gadget nodes were unreadable after the reboot; uaccess would reach that uid while it holds the active seat0 session (it does: Plasma on tty2), but nothing tags our gadget. /etc/udev/rules.d/51-android.rules (MODE 0666 for vendors 18d1, 05c6, 2717; group plugdev, absent here) came from lab-agent's connect.sh, run by hand; android-udev and systemd 262's own hwdb tags already cover adb and fastboot, and none of it covers block or tty. usb_storage and cdc_acm could not load today until the host was rebooted into its installed kernel (the running kernel's modules were gone). The aarch64 musl Rust toolchain in ~/.local/share/devlab-cross (health/build.sh) is unrecorded hand work. devlab-watch@ units come from lab-machine setup/devlab-watch.sh, enabled by hand per device (surya yes, walleye no). The host's own tools are hand copies: ~/.local/bin/land (from grenudi/lab-machine bin/land), oco-work (its only tracked home is creation-guidelines/lab-agent oco-agent/tools/oco-work, a place that is retiring), devlab and its .before-* copies; agent-env is sourced from the ideal-agent clone or plugin; tad and ikb by their install scripts; nothing names their versions. Root is only `sudo -n lab-agent root-exec --` (devlab reads DEVLAB_ROOT); ideal-agent's 2026-11-17-lab-agent-retires-by-parts part 6 moves it to a lab-root wrapper in lab-machine or narrower per-command grants, written by the author and root. walleye's device.toml already declares [host] modules usb_storage, cdc_acm and [[host.gadget]] serial walleye-first-boot, access block and tty (lab PR 54); devlab ignores the table (no deny_unknown_fields at the top). Session logs show root-exec used by hand today for fastboot devices, pacman -S (git send-email's perl modules), the host reboot, and ssh to the phone.
OUTSIDE. Nobody derives host rules from per-device declarations. LAVA declares per-device serials in data but ships one static rule calling a privileged helper; labgrid matches udev properties at run time and leaves rules to the administrator; pmbootstrap writes no rules and runs flashers as root in its chroot (whole-command doas/sudo/run0, no dry plan, a teardown verb); android-udev-rules grants MODE 0660, GROUP adbusers and TAG uaccess in one line at 51; NixOS merges rule files from many modules by name and puts extraRules at 99, too late for uaccess; Ansible's check mode is the dry plan with a diff. systemd (source and NEWS): uaccess grants only the seat's active session, so ssh-only users and services get nothing; a rule setting it must sort before 73 and must not be add-only since 258; 258+ tags ADB and fastboot by itself; 260 adds xaccess-debug-appliance for headless sessions asking through PAM; only GROUP/MODE covers services. `udevadm trigger --action=change` re-applies GROUP, MODE and uaccess to present nodes, no replug.
TAKEN. A rule file per device below 73, ACTION!="remove", matching the gadget serial on the parent (ATTRS{serial}), TAG+="uaccess"; a lab group with MODE 0660 later for a headless host; nothing by vendor for adb/fastboot (systemd covers it, a check proves it); a plan that is a content diff per file plus the exact root commands, the verb writing, reloading and triggering change only where it touched; modules-load.d only for declared modules, with "the running kernel has no modules: reboot" said by the plan; root by one prefix and a printed fixed list of commands, the list a narrow grant is written from.

brief: device.toml has three parsers and no one schema; a schema projected from one set of Rust types gives editor and CI checks at a day's cost; device crates would reverse the-phone-is-data
question: How should a device declare what it needs (its pieces, [host]) so the compiler and rust-analyzer check it: typed Rust per device, TOML with a generated schema, or serde as now?
found:
The author's question (2026-11-18, via the coordinator): no config files if possible - declarations rust and LSP-workable, relatable by machine, not in someone's head or a drifting manual. What is: device.toml is read by three crates in three shapes - devlab/src/device.rs (no deny_unknown_fields at the top or in flash, overlay, provision, install, connection: a misspelled [[flash.overlays]] is silently ignored, though the template's header says unknown fields are refused), host/src/lib.rs ([device] codename, [host] strictly, [tools] lpoco and [fastboot] serial loosely from a toml::Value) and bringup/src/boot.rs ([boot] only); no one declaration says what the file may hold. argenv (rust-with-argenv) declares an input once in code as the accessor and projects it to a published contract; its README names a hand-written sidecar schema as what drifts. Research bringup-home-follow-and-rhizoid: a tool is followed by a pin, device parts live beside it as data, hooks, or a rust-script on the pinned library; decision 2026-11-17-the-phone-is-data keeps device labs data only.
Options. (A) A typed Rust declaration per device (a crate of consts the tool links, or a rust-script on the pinned lpoco library): rename and go-to-definition across devices, errors at build - but every device change becomes a build of the device's code at the lab, the device crate pins a 0.x library, the lab would run code from each device repository, and the-phone-is-data is reversed. (B) TOML whose schema is projected from one set of Rust types (schemars, draft-07; deny_unknown_fields becomes additionalProperties false, doc comments become hover text), published per lpoco release, named on the file's first line (#:schema, taplo / Even Better TOML: completion, validation, hover), checked in CI of lab-tools (the committed schema equals the types) and of each device repository (its device.toml against the pinned schema) - the argenv way for a file: declared in code, projected, never written twice. No jump from a TOML key to its Rust field (JSON Schema carries no source location); x-taplo links can point at the field's docs. confique adds a template generated from the types (the device-template file cannot drift) but no schema, and would rewrite the types. Kconfig is the same split (typed schema, plain values, a checker); Nix modules check at evaluation. (C) Today: caught at load time, on the lane, after merge - or not at all where no deny_unknown_fields stands.
Finding: B gives the machine-checked part of the author's ask at a day's cost and keeps device repositories data; A gives rename at the price of a build and foreign code per device change. What is a piece (its files, path, version) belongs in Rust in the roof; a device only names roof pieces by token, as argenv's allowed TOKENS.

brief: sxmo: backoff has no prior art; a profile service list was refused in 2024 for the wakeup-count race - stopping before a second count read answers it. Series of 3 written with a spec
question: The best fix for sxmo's 1 s suspend retry and for its device-named service stop around suspend, as upstream would take them
found:
Upstream now (sxmo-utils master 1fd7822): sxmo_autosuspend.sh reads /sys/power/wakeup_count (blocks until no wakelocks), runs the block-suspend hook (cached 10 s), writes the count, calls sxmo_suspend.sh; on failure it sleeps 1 s and loops - no backoff, while sxmo_hook_block_suspend.sh already backs off its own blockers 1..45 s. sxmo_suspend.sh stops hexagonrpcd-adsp-sensorspd only when SXMO_DEVICE_NAME is google,b4s4-sdm670 (921fa1e, 2024, its message: not fond of device code in core, the generic solution was not recommended); it is never started again. A presuspend hook existed until 89a77e6 (2023, the move to /sys/power/wake_lock).
Prior art. Backoff after failed suspends: nothing on sxmo-devel or in the history (2691b8c, 2023, made the slow checks run rarely for the same reason: they made suspend fail). Services around suspend: proycon's 2024 patch (SXMO_SUSPEND_SERVICES stopped in sxmo_suspend.sh, started after wake) was turned down by Aren Moynihan the same day because the stop runs after the wakeup count is read: any wakelock meanwhile (the LED blink takes one every 2 s) makes the written count stale and the suspend abort, so a slow stop means never suspending; device code in sxmo_suspend.sh is a last resort citing its bug. pmaports fixed the Pixel 3a for elogind with a system-sleep hook (MR 5400) and pmOS's systemd unit conflicts with suspend.target, but Sxmo suspends with rtcwake past both, so neither runs under Sxmo. surya (systemd) has its sensors daemon stopped by suspend.target and started by the lab's devlab-sensors-resume hook; under Sxmo nothing does either.
Ways: (a) a profile list stopped inside sxmo_suspend.sh - turned down 2024; (b) suspend through logind/systemd (rtcwake -m no for the alarm, then systemctl/loginctl suspend) so distro sleep hooks run - generic, but asynchronous (sxmo measures the time slept and runs postwake after rtcwake returns), the same wakeup-count race for the hooks' time, and the lab's systemctl suspend path is the one surya never came back from (try 4); (c) the profile list stopped by sxmo_autosuspend.sh after the blockers and before a SECOND read of the wakeup count, so the stop's time cannot make the count stale, started again after the suspend whether it succeeded or not - answers the 2024 objection exactly, moves the Pixel 3a case into its profile and needs a doas rule per service. Chosen (c). Backoff: double from 1 s per failure in a row to SXMO_SUSPEND_RETRY_MAX (64 s), reset after a success.
Written (fork-sxmo-utils, local clone ~/Projects/linux-phone-oco/sxmo-utils-topics): topic/sxmo-autosuspend-backoff 2bb2500, topic/sxmo-suspend-stop-by-profile 1156bb6 (on the backoff), topic/sxmo-surya-sensors-suspend 6432ef9, lab = 6432ef9; series files in this folder's patches/sxmo-utils. Test: spec/scripts/core/sxmo_autosuspend_spec.sh, 6 examples driving the loop with mocks (waits 1 2 4 .. 64 64; cap; reset after success; stop, second read, write, suspend, start; start after a failed suspend; no services: one read) - all 6 fail on master's script and pass on the series; shellcheck and editorconfig clean (the suite's 27 other failures are the host's, the same without the series).

brief: The APSS watchdog freezes in deepest sleep and upstream refuses a watchdog kept in suspend; the PMIC watchdog with its bark as a wake IRQ answers both. RFC series of 4 written
question: Which watchdog can bring back a phone whose suspend never returns, and in what form upstream (linux-watchdog) would take it
found:
Question: a way back from a suspend that does not return - the phone resets instead of hanging - that holds on the real suspend path and that upstream would take.
What is. qcom-wdt (the APSS watchdog) stops in its late suspend callback since 2019 (to avoid resets when resume comes late). surya-lab's lab-only module parameter keep_armed_in_suspend skips that stop: it bit in s2idle cycles started by rtcwake -m freeze (proven 3+ times) but not in try 4, a real systemctl suspend, where the phone stayed down an hour with no reset (surya-unreachable-after-try4). The vendor's GPL drivers, read as observed behaviour, say why: the APSS watchdog counter freezes when all cores are suspended / the deepest low-power mode is entered (watchdog_v2.c 'qcom,wakeup-enable' commit; Sony qcom_wdt_core.c). So the APSS watchdog catches a CPU stuck while running, not a system asleep with nothing waking it.
Upstream's stance. The same idea for imx2_wdt (fsl,wdt-continue-in-low-power, Dec 2025 / Jan 2026) was refused: Guenter Roeck - a watchdog reset of a suspended system makes no sense, a system that must not suspend must not suspend; Krzysztof Kozlowski - it is OS policy, not for DT. A module parameter is the same policy in another form. What has precedent: a running watchdog whose early (pretimeout) interrupt is a wake IRQ (stm32_iwdg, ma35d1_wdt: wakeup-source + dev_pm_set_wake_irq).
The better watchdog. The PMIC's own (pm8916_wdt, qcom,pm8916-wdt, child of the PON) counts on the PMIC's sleep clock outside the sleeping SoC, and its bark is a PMIC interrupt, which wakes the system as the power key does. The second-generation PON (pm8998, pm6150 = surya, pm8998 = walleye, compatible qcom,pm8998-pon) keeps the same registers 0x54-0x58 in PON_HLOS and moves POFF_REASON1 to 0xc5 (vendor qpnp-power-on.c); qcom,pon.yaml already allows a watchdog child for every PON. Mainline uses it only on pm8916; no one proposed it for gen2.
Vectors: (A) PMIC watchdog kept running through suspend only when its bark may wake the system (DT wakeup-source = capable; power/wakeup = the user's policy, off by default) and a pretimeout is set: the bark wakes the system, the driver pets it, a system that cannot come back is reset by the bite pretimeout seconds later - a sleeping system that can wake is never reset, which answers Roeck; the policy is in sysfs, which answers Kozlowski. (B) the same on qcom-wdt with its bark as a wake IRQ - useless if the counter freezes. (C) keep the module parameter, lab only - does not cover the real path (try 4). (D) first learn what try 4 was (a sleep with no wake vs a wedged resume) - free at the next attended window, and (A) answers both. Chosen (A), (C) stays for s2idle tries until (A) is proven, (D) folded into the proof (the PMIC bark wakes a sleep with no wake; the bite resets a wedged one).
Written (fork-linux, local worktree ~/Projects/linux-phone-oco/linux-topics, branch topic/pmic-wdt-wake-in-suspend on v7.3): 1 dt-bindings qcom,pm8998-wdt + wakeup-source; 2 pm8916_wdt gen2 POFF reason via match data; 3 keep running through suspend when may wake (wake IRQ, pet in suspend, pet a bark while suspended instead of notifying the pretimeout governor, pet on resume); 4 pm6150/pm8998 dtsi nodes, disabled (bark interrupt <0x0 0x8 6>, the pm8916 index - unverified on gen2). Built with LLVM W=1 clean, checkpatch --strict clean but for the trailer, binding passes dt-doc-validate and yamllint; RFC until the phone proves it. Unknowns, each settled by the proof: can HLOS write PON_HLOS 0x854-0x858 (or is it secure-owned); the gen2 bark bit and interrupt index; POFF_REASON1 bit 2 on gen2; whether the bark wakes from suspend through PDC. Test: tests/pmic-wdt-way-back.sh (check, bite, wake) in this folder, tests pmic-wdt-bites and pmic-wdt-wakes-in-suspend.

brief: Only copybara (JVM) carries root-level files down and changes up; layered projects share four rules: one owner per file, named overrides with a status, fatal pins, a scheduled integrator report
question: What exists in the world for a chain of repositories that share files and must let changes travel both ways - subtree, submodules, josh, copybara, gbp-pq/quilt, stgit, topgit, Nix inputs, Yocto layers, Android repo, Gentoo/Arch overlays, copier/cruft, the kernel's maintainer trees - and what does each cost here (Python refused, Rust with argenv the house way)?
found:
Down and up, root-level files: subtree and subrepo carry a whole directory both ways (split/push) but need a prefix, and tad reads its statements at the root; submodules pin a repository at a path, no files at the root. Android repo copies files outside any project's history (Python). Nix inputs live in the store and cannot be patched in place (nix#3920); update-flake-lock bumps only. copier/cruft: pin + "behind" and "edited" checks, down only, Python. Renovate, multi-gitter, turbolift, microplane: a pin bump or a script per repo with a PR, down only. copybara alone does both: a follower's PR becomes a change request on the source, GitOrigin-RevId records the import, check_last_rev_state fails when the destination changed, merge_import keeps a destination's own lines - at the cost of a JVM 21 and Starlark per workflow. josh (Rust) selects single files at the root (::f, ::dest=src) and pushes back through a view, but its truth is one monorepo and a follower cannot keep its own variant; push back from separate repositories is unknown. No Rust or shell tool does root-level slices both ways: idealkb's follow.sh is the house's answer and the gap is real.
Layering: Yocto (oe-core, distro, BSP): one owner per recipe, overrides as named .bbappend files, a dangling append an error, LAYERSERIES_COMPAT fatal, Upstream-Status required on every patch and an error by default, yocto-check-layer forbids a BSP changing others' signatures - the middle layer owns the contract the lowest is checked against. Gentoo: masters non-transitive (each overlay names every ancestor, as each base here pins each source), MasterPackageClobbered an error (check-one-owner). DEP-3: Forwarded/Applied-Upstream on each patch, yet 9.4% forwarded in trixie - a status that only warns moves nothing. Kernel: upstream first, a copy says "commit X upstream", linux-next merges every tree on a schedule and mails each conflict to its owners; ACK tags every carried commit UPSTREAM/BACKPORT/FROMGIT/FROMLIST/ANDROID. stgit (Rust 2.7.0) rebases a topic and empties what upstream took; topgit merges along .topdeps, dormant; git cherry finds a landed patch by patch-id with nothing installed. b4, gbp, copier, repo are Python.
Take: a file has one owner, at the layer that owns its meaning (the contract's reader); an override is named and carries an upstream status, and a missing one fails; upstream first - a change is made at the owner and comes down by the pin; a follower's edit becomes a change request on the source (copybara); a scheduled integrator report names each drift to its owner (linux-next); landed patches retire by patch-id. Set aside every tool as a runtime: the house mechanism already lays slices, the gaps are the rules.

brief: The PMIC wdt probe wrote the S2 reset type while S2 may run, with no disable, wait or read-back; the likely cause of walleye's power-off bite. Fixed as patch 5/5 (f5bb57d27).
question: Why did the pm8916_wdt bite power off a PM8998 (walleye) instead of hard-resetting it, and how should a driver set the S2 reset type on gen2 PON?
found: Same register (+0x56/+0x57) and the same type encoding on both generations; no SEC_ACCESS needed. Every Qualcomm S2 path disables S2, waits about 10 sleep-clock cycles, writes the type, then re-enables; the probe did not, and the msm8998 firmware arms the PMIC watchdog, so the firmware's type (maybe SHUTDOWN) could stay. Other candidates: the boot chain powering off on a PMIC_WD power-on, or the platform wanting DVDD_HARD_RESET 0x08. Unread on the phone: the firmware's S2_CTL value.

brief: Any general aarch64 distro will do: a phone needs a device layer, not an OS; on Nura ~0 of it is ours for surya, on Debian ~8 small packages, Fedora ~9, ALARM ~13; walleye's is ours anywhere
question: Why a mobile distribution at all: what does a phone need beyond a general aarch64 distribution, which of it is device layer we carry anyway and which is OS burden, how big is that layer on ALARM, Debian, Fedora against Nura, and what only a mobile distribution gives?
found:
The author is right: a phone needs no special OS, only a device layer, and that layer is carried by someone on any base. Measured 2026-11-19 (pmaports main; Repology).
What a phone needs beyond a general aarch64 systemd distribution, each marked:
- Kernel + dtb per SoC/device - DEVICE LAYER. Nura carries surya's (linux-postmarketos-qcom-sm7150, sm7150-mainline tags); Mobian has 6.18 in staging; elsewhere ours. walleye's is ours on every base, Nura included.
- Boot glue - DEVICE LAYER. surya: U-Boot from sm7150-mainline flashed once, then systemd-boot EFI, which kernel-install updates on any systemd base - near generic. walleye: Android boot.img v0 with appended dtb; a kernel upgrade must rewrite the boot partition: Nura's boot-deploy does it, on a general base a kernel-install plugin of ours.
- Firmware - DEVICE LAYER: firmware-xiaomi-surya and the ath10k board files (sm7150-mainline); the generic part (adreno, qca) is in linux-firmware on every base.
- Qualcomm userspace - BASE where packaged: qrtr, rmtfs, tqftpserv, qbootctl in Debian 13, Fedora 45, Alpine 3.24; AUR-only on Arch. pd-mapper is in the kernel now (no base packages it). hexagonrpcd: Alpine only (AUR) - device layer elsewhere.
- UCM and udev/UPower/wireplumber config - DEVICE LAYER: surya's UCM is sm7150-mainline's fork (alsa-ucm-conf-qcom-sm7150); the config is soc-qcom's few files.
- ModemManager, feedbackd, callaudiod, iio-sensor-proxy - BASE: in Debian 13, Arch, Fedora 45 and Alpine 3.24 alike.
- Phone glue only Nura has: bootmac, swclock-offset, msm-firmware-loader, msm-modem-uim-selection, the call-audio idle workaround, make-dynpart-mappings, unl0kr; q6voiced Alpine only, 81voltd Debian and Alpine. Small scripts - DEVICE LAYER on a general base. This, plus someone keeping the device packages, is all only a mobile distribution gives.
- Initramfs - DEVICE LAYER at most: dracut, mkinitcpio, initramfs-tools or mkosi-initrd boot a UFS root; Nura's adds a USB-gadget debug shell, unl0kr unlock and first-boot resize (systemd-repart/growfs elsewhere). walleye already has its own (lpoco-bringup).
- Image builder - DEVICE LAYER config, a general tool: pmbootstrap for Nura; mkosi covers Debian, Arch and Fedora (not Alpine).
OS burden proper - what a distribution's maintainers carry and we carry on none of these bases: the toolchain and bootstrap; thousands of general packages with their security fixes; releases, upgrade paths, end of life; archive-wide build, mirrors and signing; installer and base images; archive QA and users' reports. We take a piece of it only by forking the base's tree, patching a general package we must rebase (sxmo-utils@lab was one; decision 2026-11-19-hardware-test-layer retires it), or holding a base past its end of life.
Size of our device layer for surya: Nura ~0 packages (it carries ~13: device, kernel, firmware x2, UCM, soc-qcom with modem and qbootctl, hexagonrpcd, msm-modem, q6voiced, bootmac, swclock-offset, ramdisk/boot-deploy); Debian ~8 (kernel, firmware, UCM, config, hexagonrpcd, q6voiced, bootmac, swclock-offset) plus a deb lane; Fedora ~9 (also 81voltd) plus an rpm lane; Arch Linux ARM ~13 (also qrtr, rmtfs, tqftpserv, qbootctl), the pacman lane exists. walleye: the kernel, dtb, firmware, UCM, boot.img glue and initramfs are ours on every base; Nura saves it the Qualcomm daemons, glue scripts and boot.img rewrite.
With sxmo dropped for a bare tty test layer, the hardware layer needs only kernel, firmware, the Qualcomm daemons, ModemManager, ALSA and lpoco - in every general base - and the last tie to Alpine (sxmo's upstream tracks Alpine; Debian has 1.12) goes.

brief: Asahi ships one device family to 5 distros by one upstream Makefile of install targets and thin hand recipes per distro; nfpm packs apk/deb/rpm/pkg from one YAML; kernel-install covers EFI boot glue
question: How do others keep one device family's layer (kernel, dtb, firmware, UCM, config, boot glue) for several distributions at once - Asahi, Pocketblue, Mobian/Debian, pmaports, mkosi, kernel-install, nfpm/fpm/OBS - and what does it teach us?
found:
Read at source 2026-11-19 (material research/base-distro/2026-11-19-agnostic-layer/).
Asahi Linux, the strongest prior art (one device family on Fedora, Arch, Gentoo, Debian, NixOS): nothing is generated across formats. Each piece has one upstream repository with a plain Makefile of small install targets and per-distribution bundles (asahi-scripts: install, install-dracut, install-mkinitcpio, install-udev-hwdb, install-fedora, install-arch); each distribution keeps a thin hand-written recipe calling one target (Fedora %make_install install-fedora; asahi-alarm make install-arch from a fork 4 commits ahead; Gentoo's ebuild the pieces one by one; Debian patched in install-debian, never merged; NixOS skips it). The one cross-format check is Packit: every upstream commit builds the Fedora spec in COPR; asahi-alarm follows Fedora's versions. One boot script (update-m1n1), a different trigger per base: kernel-install plus rpm triggers, dpkg triggers and postinst.d, a libalpm hook, extraFiles. Firmware is never packaged: extracted from macOS at install. A written policy: Fedora flagship; an alternative is listed only if its own maintainers back it, it ships all 8 named packages, takes new versions within 2 weeks, installs the normal way and supports its users; disendorsement otherwise. What hurt: a 1000+ patch kernel fork rebased weekly by one person (now shifting to upstream-first), a stale installer, Debian still without kernel and Mesa.
Pocketblue (Fedora Atomic phones): bootc, a device directory with a build script, all RPMs in one repo built into per-SoC COPRs, the kernel swapped by a same-named package. Mobian: debos, per-SoC TOML (sm7150.toml lists surya, boot.img offsets), sm7150-support -> kernel + qcom-support-common; gives back through DebianOnMobile (qcom-phone-utils, droid-juicer, pd-mapper, mkbootimg in Debian; kernels stay Mobian's). qcom-phone-utils' zz-qcom-bootimg rewrites the flashed boot.img with the dtb appended - walleye's boot glue, already in Debian. pmaports: device/firmware/linux/ucm/soc packages; deviceinfo is the nearest one-description of a phone (pmbootstrap, mkinitfs, boot-deploy, deviceinfo-converter already emits Lomiri's format); nobody uses it on another base.
mkosi: one config tree with Distribution matches; supports Fedora, Debian, Arch, openSUSE and Nura (edge only; source mkosi-distributions' not-Alpine is out of date); systemd builds itself for six bases under mkosi, each from a native recipe. kernel-install: /usr/lib/kernel/devicetree names the dtb under /usr/lib/modules/VER/dtb/ (kernel-install(8), systemd 262) - surya's EFI boot glue as one data file on Fedora, Debian with systemd-boot, Arch; Alpine runs kernel-hooks.d instead, Nura mkinitfs and boot-deploy. nfpm v2.49.0 packs prebuilt files into apk, archlinux, deb, ipk, rpm from one YAML with per-format overrides and signing; compiles nothing; repository indexes and apk-tools v3 not known yet. fpm: deb, rpm, pacman, apk module. OBS: one native recipe per family, APKBUILD since 2024-11.
Vectors: (1) declared once in Rust, packed per format by nfpm - chosen; (2) Asahi's Makefile with hand recipes per device per format; (3) native recipes generated and built per base (mkosi/OBS); (4) image-only overlays; (5) each distribution's own tree.

brief: Distro-agnostic device layer: recommended (declared once in device.toml [layer], packed per format by nfpm, apk then deb, upstream first), waits the author; 14 items; the failing test fails
question: Where does the distro-agnostic device layer stand, and what is the path for whoever takes it?
found:
How it stands, 2026-11-19 (run agnostic-layer-research.r1). Recommended, waiting on the author's word: decision 2026-11-19-device-layer-declared-once - each phone's device layer declared once in device.toml [layer] (lpoco-manifest types and schema), packed per format by lpoco layer pack through nfpm, apk first and deb second, rpm and archlinux when asked; the base stays postponed and becomes a choice of repository once the deb installs and boots. Prior art: research device-layer-agnostic-prior-art (Asahi: one upstream Makefile of install targets, thin hand recipes per distribution, Packit building the flagship's spec, upstream-first as the cure for its fork).
Cost per format (estimates): generated for every device - file lists, dependency names via a token map, systemd presets, initramfs drop-ins for four tools, deviceinfo, kernel-install's devicetree file. brief: No open base is keyed by part number for any product: mainline (compatible) is the shared home, the rest key by SoC, board or device; docs fills only the gap, linking up
question: Is there already an open, shared base for per-chip knowledge (any product: phones, boards, laptops, cars, MCUs) that we can add to, how does one add to each, and what does none of them hold?
found: No open base is keyed by part number for any product. Knowledge of a chip lives in several homes, each keyed by something else. (1) Mainline Linux is the real shared result and is product-agnostic. Its key is the devicetree compatible: the driver, the YAML binding (checked by dt_binding_check) and MAINTAINERS. U-Boot reuses the same bindings, and Zephyr reuses the convention. A chip's series goes by mail: the dt-bindings patch first, then the driver, then each board's dts apart through the SoC tree. A person signs off; the kernel accepts AI-assisted work that a human signs. (2) linux-firmware takes a blob only with its maker's licence, so board tunings such as TAS2557's stay on the product. (3) Some homes key by SoC or board. linux-msm/mainline-status (per Qualcomm SoC and PMIC block; pm8998 haptics and watchdog N/A) takes pull requests. KernelCI and LAVA key by board and SoC. Asahi, linux-sunxi and Armbian key by family. The panel generator and linux-panel-drivers key by panel. (4) Some homes key by device. The postmarketOS wiki (now Nura) is author-only: Nura forbids AI-made contributions. LineageOS blob lists are a cheap fingerprint of the chips fitted, not proof. hw-probe keys by PCI/USB ids. (5) LKDDb indexes compatible to driver per kernel release. It is generated, takes no contributions, and cannot hold a chip with no driver. (6) None holds these things: how far a chip's driver got across homes (mainline, in review, fork, downstream, none), chips with no driver, the boards carrying a part across products, firmware provenance, quirks for a second board, or the procedure and proofs that brought it up. That is the gap a thin part-number row fills, linking up and never copying. Two corrections came out of this reading. TAS2557 is in review upstream (Boiano v3, 2026-07-17, binding and driver, reviewed by Mark Brown 07-19), which walleye's port from porthole did not know. Neither porthole's TAS2557 nor its DRV2624 patch has a binding, which is the first patch either series needs. DRV2624 has no driver upstream anywhere. A second product carries it (shift-otter).

Today: surya-builder starts read builder.md from the docs clone 41 behind and missed their own row (docs 643); a walleye keeper ran its picking query in google-walleye-lab 64 behind and redid the finished TAS2557 item. Measured since 2026-11-18 12:00: the role hook already fetches the brief from origin/main (ideal-agent 0.3.28), but in 203 of 333 starts its output is over the app's hook-output cap and only a 2 KB preview arrives, so 200 of 333 starts read the brief again from the stale disk copy; 5 of 253 lane sessions ran their first picking query in a shared clone (phone-keeper.md lists the start commands before its worktree recipe). surya-coordinator.md starts in the shared surya-lab clone; coordinator.md says "at origin/main" with no command. Already right: builder, research, patrol, wakers (fresh worktree), lpoco host (reads origin/main), land's stale-tree guard (write side), the guard refusing writes in a shared clone. Every lane clone's origin/main is fresh locally (each worktree add fetches through it), so HEAD..origin/main without network names every incident. The built host-clones-fresh timer would have caught docs but not walleye (on branch build/tad-0.7.1) nor surya-lab (detached). The world: CI and agent tooling give each job a fresh tree at a SHA; GitOps reads the ref, not a tree; fail-closed version checks (If-Match, resourceVersion, force-with-lease) enforce it; nobody fast-forwards a tree in use except git-sync's one-writer symlink shape. One checkout many agents read is the anti-pattern; the fix is reading main, enforced, with a refresher only as a convenience.
